metadata.note: Santa Fe's Chicago-Los Angeles flagship trains, the historical predecessors of Amtrak's Southwest Chief (which descends directly from the Super Chief name). Route geometry is taken from the modern Amtrak route's own GTFS-sourced alignment for this corridor (see amtrak.geojson), since the historical train ran the same physical line; any place where the historical routing differed is described in the segment notes and reflected in the geometry. Era boundaries follow real, sourced milestones (train introductions, renamings, mergers, discontinuation dates); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not from real timetables. Also includes the San Francisco Chief, whose southern 'Plains line' routing through Wichita, Amarillo and Clovis differs from the Super Chief's Raton Pass main line; its geometry was rebuilt on 2026-08-26 and is now routed end to end on real OpenStreetMap track rather than hand-placed waypoints -- see its geometry_quality. The Chief and Super Chief features still use the Amtrak-sourced alignment described above. REFINEMENT (2026-08-18): the Wellington, KS - Amarillo, TX stretch originally had only two intermediate waypoints (Waynoka and Canadian) drawn as three ~150km straight lines. It now follows the real intermediate towns on the Southern Kansas Railway line the Santa Fe built in 1886-88 - Attica, Kiowa, Waynoka, Woodward, Canadian, Miami, Pampa, White Deer and Panhandle - matching the railroad's own First District (Waynoka-Canadian) and Second District (Canadian-Amarillo). Still hand-placed town waypoints, not surveyed track centerline.
metadata.source: Wikipedia (Super Chief, El Capitan, Chief), american-rails.com
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: The San Francisco Chief's stop list beyond the towns used to anchor its trace is not established, and its headway and speed remain estimates.

properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: The San Francisco Chief was introduced Jun 6 1954 - Santa Fe's last new streamliner, its first direct Chicago-San Francisco Bay train, the only Chicago-Bay Area train running over a single railroad, and at 2,555 miles the longest run in the country on one railroad. Instead of the Super Chief's Raton Pass route it swung south from Kansas City through Wichita, Amarillo and Clovis, rejoining the main line at Dalies west of Belen, then ran Barstow-Bakersfield-Stockton to Richmond. It was the last passenger train ever to serve Amarillo, ending with Amtrak's creation May 1 1971; Amtrak did not keep the route, and Amarillo has had no passenger service since. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:
Wikipedia (Super Chief, El Capitan, Chief), american-rails.com

properties.geometry_quality: RE-TRACED 2026-08-26. The previous geometry was a 127-point waypoint sketch drawing 2,241 miles as straight lines between town centres: 93% of its length sat in hops longer than 5 miles, the longest a single 169-mile leap, and Barstow to Bakersfield was one straight 117-mile line that missed Mojave by 85 km -- leaving the Tehachapi climb off the map entirely. Every mile is now routed on real OpenStreetMap track. The full trace ran 35,402 points and 2,503.3 miles against a documented 2,555 (2.0% under, the difference being terminal trackage at Dearborn Station and Richmond plus slack at the assembly joints); it is stored Douglas-Peucker simplified at 100 m -- 1311 points, 2495.9 miles -- which is three times finer than the ~300 m used for the Amtrak layer and costs 0.3% of length. Maximum deviation of the stored line from the full trace is 100 m by construction, verified at 100 m by sampling. Of 29 checked stations, 28 sit within 3 km of the line; the largest offset is 6.8 km at Chicago. ASSEMBLED IN THREE PARTS. East (Chicago-Kansas City, 443.9 mi): BNSF Chillicothe and Marceline Subdivision route relations, plus a corridor pull of raw ways for Marceline-Kansas City, where the Marceline relation is internally fragmented. Middle (Kansas City-Belen, 890.9 mi): no railway route relations exist anywhere in Kansas, Oklahoma, the Texas panhandle or eastern New Mexico, so this is routed over raw railway ways pulled as a 15 km corridor and threaded through Ottawa, Emporia, Wichita, Wellington, Waynoka, Woodward, Canadian, Pampa, Amarillo, Clovis, Fort Sumner, Vaughn and Mountainair -- including the Abo Canyon stretch of the Belen Cutoff, which needed its own tile pull. West (Belen-Richmond, 1,168.1 mi): BNSF Gallup, Seligman, Needles, Mojave, Bakersfield and Stockton Subdivision relations plus the Richmond Industrial Lead, with Barstow and Bakersfield yard trackage pulled separately to bridge where consecutive subdivision relations do not share nodes. The three parts join within 155 m and 587 m. ERA CAVEAT: this is modern track geometry standing in for a 1954-71 alignment. The corridor is the one the train used and is in service end to end today, but yard throats, station approaches and any realignment since 1971 are today's, not the Santa Fe's. Note also that the Santa Fe reached Wichita on its own line; the modern BNSF transcon bypasses Wichita via Newton, so the Emporia-Wellington leg deliberately follows the historic Wichita routing rather than the present-day through route. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 29 ruled segments totalling 433 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).
